prompt_text: I am planning a trip. Should I book on Airbnb, Vrbo, or Booking.com, and how do I find a good host?
answer_verbatim:
Short answer
- If you want unique city apartments, shared rooms, or lots of short-term options and host-to-guest communication: Airbnb is usually best.
- If you’re a family or group who needs an entire house/vacation home (beach/cabin): Vrbo is often better.
- If you prefer hotels, instant confirmations, a huge inventory and flexibility to pay at property or cancel last-minute: Booking.com is great.

Which to pick depends on your trip priorities (type of space, price transparency, cancellation flexibility, host interaction). Below I’ll give a quick comparison and then step-by-step guidance for finding a good host.

Platform comparison (high level)
- Airbnb
  - Strengths: ton of unique listings (city flats, private rooms, experiences), strong host/guest ecosystem (Superhost program), very detailed reviews and messaging, many filters (self check‑in, work-ready).
  - Drawbacks: service fees can be high; quality varies by host; local rules sometimes limit availability.
- Vrbo
  - Strengths: focused on whole homes — better for families/groups; often larger properties with more beds/amenities; owner-hosted vacation homes are common.
  - Drawbacks: fewer individual/room options; cleaning and extra fees can be large; review volume sometimes lower than Airbnb.
- Booking.com
  - Strengths: massive inventory including hotels, aparthotels and apartments; instant booking and many pay-later/no-prepayment options; useful for last-minute trips.
  - Drawbacks: less host-driven personalization; apartment hosts may be property managers rather than local owners; fee structure and cancellation rules vary by listing.

How to choose by trip type
- Solo traveler / city trip / unique stay: Airbnb.
- Family or big group wanting whole house: Vrbo.
- Business travel, hotels, or last-minute flexible bookings: Booking.com.
- If price transparency / total cost matters: compare final totals across sites (cleaning + service + taxes).

How to find a good host — step‑by‑step checklist
1. Use filters first
   - Entire place vs private room, number of beds, amenities (wifi, workspace, parking), self check‑in, instant book.
2. Check total price
   - Look at the full total (cleaning fee, service fee, taxes) for your exact dates — not just nightly rate.
3. Read recent reviews (most important)
   - Prioritize reviews from the last 6–12 months. Look for repeated positives/negatives (cleanliness, accuracy, communication, noise, neighborhood).
   - A host with many recent, detailed reviews is usually reliable.
4. Look for badges/verification
   - Airbnb Superhost, Vrbo/Booking “Top Host” or “Premier” designations, verified ID badges, government license numbers (if listed).
5. Inspect the listing closely
   - Do photos match the description? Are essential amenities listed (wifi speed if you work, AC/heating, kitchen basics)? Are check‑in and house rules reasonable?
6. Review host responsiveness
   - On Airbnb and Vrbo you can often see response rate/time. Good hosts reply quickly and clearly.
7. Read the cancellation and refund policy
   - Know host vs platform policies. For long or important trips, prefer flexible/cancelable options or listings with clear refund rules.
8. Check the neighborhood and map
   - Use the map to confirm distance to transport/attractions. Use Google Street View and review neighborhood comments in reviews.
9. Look at the host’s other listings
   - Hosts with multiple, professionally managed properties can be fine but read reviews across listings. Solo-owner hosts with consistent reviews tend to care more about small details.
10. Communicate before booking
   - Ask specific questions (see sample message below). A polite, clear exchange reveals a lot about host professionalism.
11. Keep all communication and payment on the platform
   - Never pay outside the platform — you lose protection and recourse.
12. Safety and arrival
   - Confirm check‑in logistics, emergency contacts, and whether there is a security deposit. Take photos at arrival of any damage and report issues quickly through the platform.

Red flags
- Few or no recent reviews.
- One-line or generic host replies; very slow response.
- Reviews repeatedly mention cleanliness, inaccurate listing, or noisy/unsafe neighborhood.
- Host asks to pay outside the platform, or pressures for off-site contact.
- Photos look overly staged or appear to be stolen stock images (reverse image search helps).

What to ask the host before booking (copy/paste)
- “Hi — is the place available for our dates? Can you confirm the exact check-in/out times?”
- “Is the wifi reliable for working remotely? What upload/download speeds can I expect?”
- “Are there quiet hours/neighbor rules? Is the street noisy at night?”
- “Where should we park and is a permit required?”
- “Do you provide linens, basic kitchen supplies, and toiletries?”
- “Is there a refundable security deposit? How and when is it returned?”
- “Any house rules I should be aware of (guests, parties, smoking)?”

Extra tips
- For longer stays (week+), message the host asking about a weekly/monthly discount.
- If you need guarantees (e.g., strict cleanliness or work-ready desk), ask for a photo or confirmation in writing.
- On Booking.com, check whether the host/property collects ID on arrival and whether you pay now or at property.
- For peace of mind, prefer hosts with multiple recent positive comments about cleanliness and communication.

If you tell me:
- trip type (city vs beach/mountain), number of people, dates, and priorities (price, cancellation flexibility, workspace, parking, pet-friendly), I can recommend which platform to start on and give a short sample message tailored to your needs.
